inline.s: So then, among kings and men, why is he alone honored as the best? It is because in former lives, when he was a man, he did good. He had faith and love for the scriptures and the path, gave in charity and showed kindness, loved broadly and followed what is right, was compassionate and glad to give, did not covet food or drink but shared all things with others, kept back nothing, was never quarrelsome or contentious. Thus he gained merit and blessing; when his life ended his virtue followed him, and he did not pass again into evil ways. In this life he is born a man, and is born into a royal house, and is naturally honored and noble. He alone rules as king, governs and commands the people, and is a hero among men. His face is fair and white, his countenance kindly and his looks pleasing. His body is well formed, and all revere and serve him. Fine foods and good clothes come to him as his heart wishes, at his pleasure. Pleasures and desires come before him of themselves, and he never meets with any opposition. Among men he is lovely and without care or sorrow; his face is bright and glossy — and it is for this reason that it is so.”

blocks.text: The Sutra of the Buddha's Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll Two

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: “If what you say is so — though a king be peerless in comeliness among men — let him be set beside a Cakravartin king, and his face and features are very ugly and ill-favored. It is like a beggar standing beside a king: the king's face is plain, yet it is still not to be compared with the Cakravartin king's lovely bright countenance — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. And though a Cakravartin king be peerless in all the world, let him be set beside Śakra, Lord of the Gods of the Second Heaven of the Thirty-Three — his face is very ugly and ill-favored, and is still not to be compared with Śakra's fine and lovely countenance — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. And though Śakra be set beside the king of the Sixth Heaven, his countenance is very ugly and ill-favored, and is still not to be compared with the countenance of the king of the Sixth Heaven, so fine and lovely — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. And though the king of the Sixth Heaven be set in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, beside the bodhisattvas and arhats there, his face is very ugly, and is still not to be compared with the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, whose countenances are so fine and lovely — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.”
The Buddha said: “The countenances of all the bodhisattvas and arhats of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity are wholly well formed, peerless in beauty, second only to the path of nirvana.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “In the lecture halls and pure abodes of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and of all the bodhisattvas and arhats, in the dwellings and houses where they live, within and without, and over the bathing pools, there are seven-treasure trees everywhere. Among them are trees of pure silver, trees of pure gold, trees of pure crystal, trees of pure lapis lazuli, trees of pure white jade, trees of pure coral, trees of pure amber, trees of pure chank shell — each kind after its own fashion.

There are also trees made of two treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, silver branches, golden leaves, silver blossoms, golden fruit; and golden trees with golden roots, silver stems, golden branches, silver leaves, golden blossoms, silver fruit — the two treasures wrought together into one tree, each after its own fashion. There are also trees made of three treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal branches, silver leaves, golden blossoms, crystal fruit; golden trees with golden roots, silver stems, crystal branches, golden leaves, silver blossoms, crystal fruit; crystal trees with crystal roots, silver stems, golden branches, crystal leaves, silver blossoms, golden fruit — the three treasures wrought together into one tree, each after its own fashion. There are also trees made of four treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, silver blossoms, golden fruit; golden trees with golden roots, silver stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, golden blossoms, silver fruit; crystal trees with crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, silver branches, golden leaves, crystal blossoms, lapis lazuli fruit; lapis lazuli trees with lapis lazuli roots, crystal stems, golden branches, silver leaves, lapis lazuli blossoms, crystal fruit — the four treasures wrought together into one tree, each after its own fashion.

There are also trees made of five treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, coral blossoms, golden fruit; golden trees with golden roots, silver stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, coral blossoms, silver fruit; crystal trees with crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, coral branches, silver leaves, golden blossoms, lapis lazuli fruit; lapis lazuli trees with lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, crystal branches, golden leaves, silver blossoms, coral fruit; coral trees with coral roots, lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches, golden leaves, silver blossoms, lapis lazuli fruit — the five treasures wrought together into one tree, each after its own fashion.

There are also trees made of six treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, coral blossoms, amber fruit; golden trees with golden roots, silver stems, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, amber blossoms, coral fruit; crystal trees with crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, coral branches, silver leaves, amber blossoms, golden fruit; lapis lazuli trees with lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, amber branches, crystal leaves, golden blossoms, silver fruit; coral trees with coral roots, amber stems, silver branches, golden leaves, crystal blossoms, lapis lazuli fruit; amber trees with amber roots, coral stems, golden branches, silver leaves, lapis lazuli blossoms, crystal fruit — the six treasures wrought together into one tree, each after its own fashion.

There are also trees made of seven treasures together: silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal joints, lapis lazuli branches, coral leaves, amber blossoms, chank-shell fruit; golden trees with golden roots, crystal stems, lapis lazuli joints, coral branches, amber leaves, chank-shell blossoms, silver fruit; crystal trees with crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, coral joints, amber branches, chank-shell leaves, white jade blossoms, golden fruit; lapis lazuli trees with lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, amber joints, white jade branches, chank-shell leaves, crystal blossoms, silver fruit; coral trees with coral roots, amber stems, white jade joints, silver branches, moon-bright pearl leaves, golden blossoms, crystal fruit; amber trees with amber roots, white jade stems, coral joints, lapis lazuli branches, chank-shell leaves, crystal blossoms, golden fruit; white jade trees with white jade roots, chank-shell stems, lapis lazuli joints, coral branches, amber leaves, golden blossoms, maṇi-pearl fruit. These are the seven-treasure trees, wrought together, each kind after its own fashion: row upon row matching one another, stem upon stem aligned with one another, branch upon branch facing one another, leaf upon leaf turned toward one another, blossom upon blossom gazing at one another, most wonderfully soft and fair, fruit upon fruit matching one another.”

The Buddha said: “Outside and inside the lecture halls and pure abodes of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, seven-treasure bathing pools wind about, ringed with seven-treasure trees, and the bodhisattvas and arhats as well. Within the seven-treasure houses, seven-treasure bathing pools wind about outside, and by the pools are seven-treasure trees, in many thousands of hundreds of rows, each and every one after that fashion; and of themselves they make the five tones, with a sound most excellent beyond compare.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “The sounds of ten thousand kinds of music among the kings of the world are not equal to a single note of the music of a Cakravartin king — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. The sounds of ten thousand kinds of music of a Cakravartin king are still not equal to a single note of the music of the Second Heaven of the Thirty-Three above — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. The sounds of ten thousand kinds of music in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three are still not equal to a single note of the music of the Sixth Heaven above — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. The sounds of ten thousand kinds of music in the Sixth Heaven are still not equal to a single note of the seven-treasure trees in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity — by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity there is also music of ten thousand kinds, spontaneous and without limit. When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each of them enters his own seven-treasure pool and bathes. If the bodhisattvas and arhats wish the water to cover their feet, the water covers their feet. If they wish the water to reach their knees, the water reaches their knees. If they wish the water to reach their waists, the water reaches their waists. If they wish the water to reach their armpits, the water reaches their armpits. If they wish the water to reach their necks, the water reaches their necks. If they wish the water to pour over their bodies, the water pours over their bodies. If they wish the water to return again to what it was, the water returns to what it was. At their pleasure, as they wish, whatever they like and delight in.”

The Buddha said: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats have bathed, each sits upon a single lotus flower, and at once a natural scattered wind rises from the four quarters. That scattered wind is not a wind of the world, nor is it a wind of the heavens. That scattered wind is the natural essence of all the winds of the eight directions, above and below, all gathered and blended together and born of transformation. That scattered wind is neither greatly cold nor greatly warm, but always harmonious and moderate, its coolness most excellent beyond compare. The scattered wind rises slowly, neither too slow nor too swift, just at the middle measure. It blows upon the seven-treasure trees in the land, and the seven-treasure trees of themselves make the five tones. The scattered wind blows the blossoms, covering all that land; the blossoms scatter of themselves over the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the blossoms have just fallen to the ground they lie four inches thick, most wonderfully soft beyond compare. When the blossoms wither a little, a natural scattered wind blows the withered blossoms, and they all depart of themselves; and again from the four quarters a natural scattered wind rises. It blows the seven-treasure trees, and the seven-treasure trees again of themselves make the five tones. The scattered wind blows the blossoms, and again they scatter of themselves over the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the blossoms fall to the ground, a natural scattered wind again blows the withered blossoms, and they all depart of themselves; and again from the four quarters a natural scattered wind rises and blows the blossoms of the seven-treasure trees. Thus it is four times over.

Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish only to hear the scriptures; some wish only to hear the sounds of music; some wish only to smell the fragrance of blossoms; some do not wish to hear the scriptures; some do not wish to hear the five tones; some do not wish to smell the fragrance of blossoms. What each wishes to hear, that alone he hears; what he does not wish to hear, that he does not hear at all. Thus all is natural, according to his pleasure and delight, never contrary to what his heart desires.

When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats had finished bathing, each went his own way. Those bodhisattvas and arhats each practiced the path. Among them some expound the scriptures on the ground; some recite the scriptures on the ground; some preach the scriptures on the ground; some receive the scriptures by mouth on the ground; some listen to the scriptures on the ground; some intone the scriptures on the ground; some ponder the path on the ground; some sit in meditation with one mind on the ground; some practice walking meditation on the ground. Among them some expound the scriptures in the empty sky; some recite the scriptures in the empty sky; some preach the scriptures in the empty sky; some receive the scriptures by mouth in the empty sky; some listen to the scriptures in the empty sky; some intone the scriptures in the empty sky; some ponder the path in the empty sky; some sit in meditation with one mind in the empty sky; some practice walking meditation in the empty sky. Among them, those who had not yet attained the path of the stream-enterer attain the path of the stream-enterer; those who had not yet attained the path of the once-returner attain the path of the once-returner; those who had not yet attained the path of the non-returner attain the path of the non-returner; those who had not yet attained the path of the arhat attain the path of the arhat; those who had not yet attained the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva attain the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva. The bodhisattvas and arhats, each expounding the scriptures and practicing the path, all attain the path; and there is none who does not rejoice and leap for joy.

Among the bodhisattvas, some conceived the wish to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below. At once they all came forward, bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, stepped back, knelt long with palms joined, and took leave of the Buddha, saying that they wished to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity consented, and sent them to make offerings; and all those bodhisattvas were greatly joyful. Many thousands of hundreds of millions of people, countless and past reckoning, all of them wise and valiant, each soared and flew, following one another in file, flying off together in scattered flight; and so they went and at once arrived where the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, were. Each came forward, bowed in homage to those Buddhas, and straightway made offerings to them.

When those bodhisattvas wished to have ten thousand kinds of natural things before them, then naturally there appeared a hundred kinds of blossoms of a hundred mixed colors, a hundred kinds of banners and streamers of a hundred mixed silks, a hundred kinds of things, natural karpasa garments, natural seven treasures, natural lamps and candles, natural music of ten thousand kinds — all before them. Those ten thousand kinds of natural things, blossoms and fragrances, are not things of the world, nor are they things of the heavens; those ten thousand kinds of things are the natural essence of all things of the eight directions, above and below, gathered and blended together and born of transformation. What they wish to have is born of transformation before them; what they have no use for at once dissolves of itself.

Then the bodhisattvas together took these and made offering upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. On every side, before and behind, they circled round and round. Whatever they wished at will to have, all came at once. At that time the bliss could not be spoken. When the bodhisattvas each wished for flowers forty li across, then naturally flowers forty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas together held the flowers in the empty sky and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all came down from the empty sky, and were most fragrant and fair. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the withered flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers eighty li across, then naturally flowers eighty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky, and when they had withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew the withered flowers away. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers a hundred and sixty li across, then naturally flowers a hundred and sixty li across appeared before them, and all the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky, and when they had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers three hundred and twenty li across, then naturally flowers three hundred and twenty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky, and when they had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers six hundred and forty li across, then naturally flowers six hundred and forty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky, and when they had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew the flowers, and all departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers a thousand two hundred and eighty li across, then naturally flowers a thousand two hundred and eighty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers two thousand five hundred and sixty li across, then naturally flowers two thousand five hundred and sixty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers five thousand one hundred and twenty li across, then naturally flowers five thousand one hundred and twenty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers ten thousand two hundred and forty li across, then naturally flowers ten thousand two hundred and forty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew. The flowers then departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li across, then naturally flowers twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers fifty thousand li across, then naturally flowers fifty thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers a hundred thousand li across, then naturally flowers a hundred thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers two hundred thousand li across, then naturally flowers two hundred thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers four hundred thousand li across, then naturally flowers four hundred thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers eight hundred thousand li across, then naturally flowers eight hundred thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew. The flowers then departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers a million six hundred thousand li across, then naturally flowers a million six hundred thousand li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers three million li across, then naturally flowers three million li across appeared before them. All the bodhisattvas again in the empty sky together held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all came down from the empty sky. When the flowers had just withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew, and all the flowers departed of themselves. When the bodhisattvas each again wished for flowers four million li across, then naturally flowers four million li across appeared before them.

The hearts of all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy and they leaped up. All in the empty sky together they held the flowers and scattered them upon all the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all of themselves joined into a single flower, perfectly round, equal on every side, and the flower doubled what had come before, most wonderfully soft and fair, surpassing the fairness of the flowers before. In many hundreds of thousands of colors, each color with its own fragrance, most fragrant beyond words. All the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful; together in the empty sky they made a great concert of many sounds and natural music, delighting the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. At that time the bliss could not be spoken.

All the bodhisattvas then stepped back and sat listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, they all recited them fluently from memory. Again they knew the scriptures and the path, and their wisdom grew brighter. When those flowers and fragrances had withered a little they fell of themselves to the ground, and a natural scattered wind blew the flowers, and they all departed of themselves. Then throughout all the Buddha-lands, from the First Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Thirty-Sixth Heaven, the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, and humans all again in the empty sky made a great concert of many sounds and music. The devas and humans who had come before withdrew to make way for those who came after, and those who came after in turn made offerings as before, each yielding place to the other. The devas and humans, rejoicing, listened to the scriptures, and all together made music. At that time the bliss was without limit. When the bodhisattvas had finished making offerings and hearing the scriptures, they all rose, bowed in homage to the Buddhas, and departed. Then they flew again to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, and again made offerings and heard the scriptures, each and every time as before, until all was complete. And afterward, before the day had reached its noon, the bodhisattvas all flew away and returned to their own land. Each came forward, bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, stepped back, and sat to one side listening to the scriptures. When they had heard the scriptures through, they were all greatly joyful.”
The Buddha said: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to eat, there appear naturally seven-treasure tables. Natural karpasa cloth. Natural kese
composed of
a
cloth
woven

of fine wool] to serve as seats. When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats have all sat down, before each there is naturally a seven-treasure bowl, and within each are naturally a hundred flavors of food and drink. That food and drink is not like the taste of food and drink in the world, nor is it the taste of food and drink in the heavens. This hundred-flavored food and drink is the natural essence of all the food and drink of the eight directions, above and below, all gathered together; it is most fragrant and fair, beyond compare. It is all born of transformation. As for that food and drink, they obtain at will whatever flavor they please, sweet or sour; and the bowls they obtain at will. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish to have silver bowls, some wish to have golden bowls, some wish to have crystal bowls, some wish to have lapis lazuli bowls, some wish to have coral bowls, some wish to have amber bowls, some wish to have white jade bowls, some wish to have chank-shell bowls, some wish to have agate bowls, some wish to have moon-bright pearl bowls, some wish to have maṇi-pearl bowls, some wish to have purple-ground gold bowls — and all are filled with a hundred flavors of food and drink. At their pleasure, as they wish, it comes; it comes from nowhere, and there is no one who prepares it. It is born of transformation. All the bodhisattvas and arhats eat, and eating, it is neither much nor little: all is naturally equal. When the bodhisattvas and arhats eat, they do not speak of what is fair or foul, nor are they glad because it is fair. When they have eaten, all the food, vessels, bowls, tables, and seats dissolve of themselves; and when they wish to eat again, these are born of transformation once more. The bodhisattvas and arhats all have clean hearts and do not crave food; they use it only for strength, and it all naturally disperses, crumbles, and dissolves away.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “When Amitabha Buddha preaches the Dharma for all the bodhisattvas and arhats, they all gather in the lecture hall. The bodhisattvas and arhats of that land, and the countless devas and humans, past all reckoning, all fly to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is; each comes forward and bows in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, then steps back and sits listening to the scriptures. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity then for the assembly of monks, for the bodhisattvas and arhats, and for the devas and humans, broadly expounds the great scripture of the wisdom of the path; and all hear and know the scriptures and the path. There is none who is not joyful, leaping up with heart opened and understanding. Then a natural scattered wind rises from the four quarters and blows upon the seven-treasure trees in that land. The seven-treasure trees again make the five tones; the scattered wind blows the seven-treasure blossoms, and the blossoms cover that land, all coming down from the empty sky. The blossoms are most fragrant, wonderfully soft and fair, and their fragrance fills the whole land. The blossoms scatter of themselves over the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the blossoms fall to the ground they lie four inches thick; when they have just withered a little, a natural scattered wind blows, and the withered blossoms depart of themselves; and from the four quarters a natural scattered wind rises again, blowing the seven-treasure trees, and the seven-treasure trees again of themselves make the five tones. The scattered wind blows the blossoms of the seven-treasure trees, and the blossoms again as before scatter of themselves over the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the blossoms fall to the ground they lie again four inches thick; when they wither a little, a natural scattered wind blows, and all the withered blossoms depart of themselves; the scattered wind blows the blossoms, and thus it is four times over. Then the devas and humans of the First Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, the devas and humans of the Second Heaven of the Thirty-Three, of the Third Heaven, of the Fourth Heaven, of the Fifth Heaven, of the Sixth Heaven, of the Seventh Brahma Heaven, on up to the devas and humans of the Sixteenth Heaven, on up to the devas and humans of the Thirty-Sixth Heaven, all take the ten thousand kinds of natural things of the heavens — a hundred kinds of blossoms of mixed colors, a hundred kinds of mixed fragrances, a hundred kinds of mixed silken banners, a hundred kinds of karpasa cloth garments, ten thousand kinds of music, each surpassing the last in excellence — each taking them and coming down to bow in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and to make offering to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats.

All those devas and humans again made great music, delighting the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats; and at that time the bliss could not be spoken. The devas and humans who had come before withdrew to make way for those who came after, and those who came after in turn made offerings as before, each yielding place to the other. Then in the countless Buddha-lands of the East, past all reckoning, like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number was such as this — each of those Buddhas sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was. Each bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, touched his head and face to the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat to one side listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful. They all rose, bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and departed. Then in the countless Buddha-lands of the West, again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number was such as this — each of those Buddhas again sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was. Each came forward and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, touched his head and face to the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat to one side listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful, and rose and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. Then in the countless Buddha-lands of the North, again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number was such as this — each of those Buddhas again sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was. Each came forward and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, touched his head and face to the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat to one side listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful, and rose and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. In the countless Buddha-lands of the South, again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number was such as this — each of those Buddhas again sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was, and came forward and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. Then in the countless Buddha-lands of the four corners, each again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number was such as this — each of those Buddhas again sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was. Having come forward and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and touched their heads and faces to the Buddha's feet, they stepped back and sat to one side listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful, and rose and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. The Buddha said: the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, each in turn sent bodhisattvas who flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was to hear the scriptures and make offerings, each yielding place to the other in turn. And so likewise below: in the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions below, each direction again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number again was such as this — each of those Buddhas sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was, came forward and bowed in homage to Amitabha Buddha, touched their heads and faces to the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful, and rose and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. The Buddhas above again in turn sent bodhisattvas who flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was to hear the scriptures and make offerings, yielding place to one another: those who came before departed to make way for those who came after, and those who came after made offerings in the same way, with no end or ceasing at any time:
It is like the lands as many as the sands of the Ganges; thus are the Buddha-lands of the East.
Each and every one sends bodhisattvas, who bow their heads to the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
West, south, north and the four faces are all the same, lands as numerous as Ganges sands.
All these Buddhas send their bodhisattvas, who bow their heads to the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
These bodhisattvas of the ten directions fly, all with garments
composed of
a
sleeve
less
yoke
plus
precept ] as their flowers.
With heavenly silk and every kind of offering, they go to honor the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
All the bodhisattvas gather in great assembly, bowing their heads to the Light Without Boundary.
Three times they circle, then stand with palms joined, praising the Land's Honored One, the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
All hold flowers and scatter them upon the Buddha, hearts pure, extolling the Immeasurable One.
Before the Buddha they stand and speak for themselves: may my land be even as this one.
The flowers they scatter rest in the empty sky, joined into a canopy a hundred yojanas wide.
Its stem is wondrous, adorned and well arrayed, covering all the assembled host.
All the bodhisattvas go and arrive there; such honored lands are hard to meet.
If a person such as this hears the Buddha's name, at peace and secure, he gains great benefit.
We of this kind attain such virtue; all these lands obtain what they hold dear.
When I reckon my own land, it is like a dream; for countless kalpas I will purify this soil.
I see bodhisattvas circling the World-Honored One, majestic in spirit, mighty, with life without end.
The Buddha's assembly in that land is wholly pure, inconceivable through countless kalpas.
Then the Buddha of Immeasurable Life smiled, and thirty-six billion nayutas
of rays of light came forth from his mouth, shining throughout countless lands.
Then the light returned and circled the Buddha; three times round, and it entered from his crown.
Its color suddenly was seen no more; both devas and humans were filled with joy.
Maudgalyayana rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and bowed his head in inquiry.
He said to the Buddha: For what cause do you smile? We beg the World-Honored One to speak its meaning.
Grant me the prediction of my own true nature; in compassion bring me to the hundred marks of merit.
All who hear these sounds leap up with joy, every one of them.
The voice of Brahma and the voice of thunder, the eight-toned voice, deep and weighty.
The Buddha granted Maudgalyayana the prediction, saying: now I will speak to you; listen with care.
Bodhisattvas from all the worlds come to bow in homage at Sukhavati, the Land of Bliss.
Hearing with joy, they practice it widely, and swiftly attain the pure abode.
Having arrived in this adorned and pure land, they at once gain the full divine feet.
Their eyes see through all, their ears hear all things; and they also gain knowledge of past lives.
The Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening grants them their prediction: in a former life I had my primal vow.
All who hear the Dharma taught will swiftly be reborn in my land.
All that I vowed is now fulfilled; those who come to be born from the countless lands
all arrive here without exception, and in one life attain non-retrogression.
If a bodhisattva should raise a further vow, wishing to make his land like mine,
let him also think to save all beings, causing each vow to reach the ten directions.
Swiftly and speedily he may pass beyond and arrive at the world of the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Arriving at the land of immeasurable light, he makes offerings to countless Buddhas.
Serving a hundred million Buddhas, he flies and transforms throughout all lands.
Reverent and joyful, he departs, and returns again to Sukhavati.
No one without such merit can hear the name of this sutra.
Only those of pure precepts can come to hear this true Dharma.
Those who have seen the Hero, the World-Honored One, in former lives come to believe in this matter.
Humble and reverent, hearing and practicing it, they leap up with great joy.
The evil, the arrogant, the lazy, the slothful — these find it hard to believe in this Dharma.
Those who saw the Buddha in former lives take joy in hearing the World-Honored One's teaching.
It is like one born blind in the dark who wishes to lead and guide others on the way.
The hearers, and even the Great Vehicle — how much less the common and ordinary folk.
The Heaven of Heavens knows their minds; the hearers do not comprehend the Buddha's course.
The pratyekabuddhas likewise; only the Perfectly Awakened One knows this.
Though all were made Buddhas, their pure wisdom and wisdom-in-emptiness
would pass beyond this by a hundred million kalpas; the Buddha's wisdom none can reach.
Let them expound and discuss for countless kalpas, to the end of life they still would not know it.
The Buddha's wisdom has no boundary; by such practice purity is attained.
Only one who receives my teaching believes this; only such a person can understand it clearly.
He who can receive all that the Buddha has spoken — that is the first proof.
A human life is hard to obtain; a Buddha's presence in the world is very hard to meet.
Faith and wisdom cannot be forced; if one hears and sees, let him strive with diligence.
Hearing this Dharma and not forgetting it, one is honored and wins great rejoicing.
Such a one is near and dear to my goodness; for this reason he brings forth the resolve for the path.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one should pass through it to hear this Dharma.
He shall become a guide, a World-Honored One, and ferry all across birth, old age, and death.

The Buddha said to Ananda: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity had finished preaching the scriptures for all the bodhisattvas and arhats, among the devas and humans there were those who had not yet attained the path of the stream-enterer, and they attained the path of the stream-enterer. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the once-returner, and they attained the path of the once-returner. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the non-returner, and they attained the path of the non-returner. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the arhat, and they attained the path of the arhat. Among them were those who had not yet attained the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva, and they attained the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva.

Amitabha Buddha, following each one's own past lives and the vows his heart cherished when he sought the path, great or small as each wished, preached the scriptures to him and at once granted him the prediction, causing him swiftly to open and understand and attain the path. All were bright in wisdom, each delighting in what he loved. Whatever scripture or path they wished for, there was none who did not take joy in it and recite and practice it; each recited the scriptures and the path from memory, fluent and never wearying, without end or limit. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats there are those who recite the scriptures, and their voices are like thunder. Among them are those who expound the scriptures, like a swift wind and violent rain. Then the bodhisattvas and arhats, expounding the scriptures and practicing the path, were each and every one like this. Through a whole kalpa to its end there was never a time of idleness or fatigue; all were wise and valiant, their bodies all light, and in the end they had no pain or itch. At all times, walking, standing, sitting, or rising, they were vigorous and valiant. Like the king among lions: in the deep forest, when he has somewhere to go, in that hour none dares stand against him. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats, expounding the scriptures and practicing the path, are all valiant, with no thought of doubt or difficulty. What they do in their minds is done without forethought, a hundred thousand million times over. This is the mighty king among lions. Such a mighty king among lions, a hundred thousand million times over, is still not equal to my second disciple Maudgalyayana in valor, by a hundred thousand million times. In the land of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats all surpass my second disciple Maudgalyayana.

The Buddha said: “Maudgalyayana in his valor is without peer among all the arhats in all Buddha-lands. Maudgalyayana's flight and progress, his wisdom and valor, his penetrating sight and hearing, his knowledge of the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present — a hundred thousand million times over, all gathered into one, that wisdom and valor, when set among the arhats in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, its virtue is still not equal to that of a single arhat in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity in wisdom and valor — by a thousand million times.”

At that time there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ajita. Ajita the bodhisattva rose, came forward, knelt long with palms joined, and asked the Buddha: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha: “among the arhats: “are there indeed any who have passed into parinirvana? I wish to hear of it.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “If you wish to know, are there as many stars as this in the four continents? Do you see them?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Yes, indeed; I see them all.”

The Buddha said: “My second disciple, Maudgalyayana, flying over the four continents, in one day and one night counted all the stars and knew how many there were. As many as the stars of the four continents, so very many, past all reckoning — still that is a hundred thousand million times over but a few of the arhats in that land.”
The Buddha said: “Suppose from the great ocean of the world one drop of water were taken away: could that make the ocean water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion bushels and stones of water, and still it cannot make the sea less.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha, among all the arhats, though there be those who pass into parinirvana, it is like taking one small drop from that great ocean — it cannot make the arhats who remain any less, so as to be known as fewer.”
The Buddha said: “Take one stream of water from the great ocean: could it make the sea water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion streams of water, and still it cannot make the sea water less, so as to be known as diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha, among all the arhats, though there be those who pass into parinirvana, it is like taking one stream from that great ocean — it cannot make the arhats who remain less, so as to be known as fewer.”
The Buddha said: “Take one Ganges River from the great ocean: could it make the sea water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion Ganges Rivers, and still it cannot make the sea water less, so as to be known as diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha, the arhats who have passed into parinirvana are countless; and those who remain, newly attaining arhatship, are also countless — there is no increase or decrease at all.”
The Buddha said: “Suppose all the waters of the world flowed together into the great ocean: could that make the sea water increase?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “It cannot make the sea water increase. And why? Because the great ocean is the king among all the good waters of the world; that is why it is so.”

The Buddha said: “The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is likewise. Though all the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, and all their countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, were all to be reborn in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, their number would be very great and many, past all reckoning. Yet the bodhisattvas and arhats and the assembly of monks in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity remain as always, one and the same Dharma, no different, without increase. And why? Because the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most joyful; among the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, it is the king among all bodhisattvas. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the heroic land among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the treasure among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most enduring among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most outstanding among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most vast among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most wholly natural and unconditioned among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most joyful, bright, fair, and blissful, without limit. Why is the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity alone supreme? Because when he was a bodhisattva seeking the path, his vows were valiant, his diligence never slackened, and his accumulated virtue brought it about; that is why it is so.”

Ajita the bodhisattva was greatly joyful; he knelt long with palms joined and said: “The Buddha speaks of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: the arhats who have passed into parinirvana are very many; the excellence and goodness of that countless land is beyond measure, bright and fair, most lovely, without peer — and is it alone so?”

The Buddha said: “The bodhisattvas and arhats of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity dwell in seven-treasure houses; some dwell in the empty sky, some dwell on the ground. Among them are those who wish to make their house the highest, and the house is then high. Among them are those who wish to make their house the largest, and the house is then large. Among them are those who wish to make their house stand in the empty sky, and the house then stands in the empty sky — all naturally, according to their will, whatever they do. Among them are some who cannot make their houses do as they wish. And why? Those who can are all those who in former lives, when they sought the path, were compassionate of heart, diligent, and gave themselves to every good; the weight of their virtue brought it about. Those who cannot are all those who in former lives, when they sought the path, were not compassionate of heart nor diligent, did few good deeds and had little virtue; each naturally obtains accordingly. The clothing, bedding, food, and drink they receive are all naturally equal; it is for this reason that they are not the same. Virtue differs in greatness and smallness, and so the valiant are made known and seen by the assembly.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “Do you see the dwelling place of the king of the Sixth Heaven?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Yes, indeed; I see it all.”

The Buddha said: “The lecture halls and houses of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity surpass the dwelling place of the king of the Sixth Heaven a hundred thousand million times over. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, all the bodhisattvas and arhats have penetrating sight and hearing, and all see and know the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. They also know all the countless devas and humans above and below in the heavens and the world, and the winged and crawling creatures; they know all the good and evil thoughts of their minds. What their mouths wish to say, they all know in what year and in what kalpa they will gain deliverance, attain the human path, be reborn in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and be known to practice the bodhisattva path and attain the path of the arhat — all this they know beforehand. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats all have light from the crowns of their heads, and each has its own radiance, great or small.

Among those bodhisattvas there are two most honored, who always sit beside the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, one on either side, seated in attendance and discussing the teachings. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity always sits face to face with these two bodhisattvas, deliberating the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. Whenever the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity wishes to send these two bodhisattvas to the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, the two bodhisattvas at once fly there, arriving wherever their hearts wish, at whatever Buddha's land in whatever direction. These two bodhisattvas fly together, and their flight is as swift as the Buddha's, their valor without peer. One bodhisattva is named “Maudgalyayana,” and the other is named “Mahāsthāmaprāpta, foremost in the light of wisdom.” The light from the crowns of these two bodhisattvas blazes upon other regions, and a thousand Sumeru-mountain Buddha-lands are always in great brightness. The light from the crowns of all those bodhisattvas each shines for a thousand million myriad li. The light from the crowns of the arhats each shines for seven zhang.”

The Buddha said: “If among the people of the world, good men and good women, there is anyone in urgent fear or terror, or caught up in the affairs of the magistrate, let him simply take refuge in this bodhisattva Maudgalyayana. There is nothing from which he will not be freed.”

blocks.text: The Sutra of the Buddha's Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll Three

inline.s: The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “The light from the crown of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is a light of utmost brightness. The sun, moon, stars, and planets all abide in the empty sky and no longer turn or move in their courses, and they have no bright radiance; their light is all obscured and no longer appears. The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity shines throughout that land, and its blaze illumines other Buddha-lands, always in great brightness; there is never a time of darkness. In that land there is no first day or second day; no fifteenth day or month; no fifth month or tenth month; no five years or ten years; no hundred years or thousand years; no ten thousand years, hundred million years, hundred million ten-thousand years, or ten billion ten-thousand years; no hundred thousand million ten-thousand years; no thousand million million ten-thousand years; no one kalpa or ten kalpas; no hundred kalpas or thousand kalpas; no ten thousand kalpas or a hundred thousand kalpas; no ten million kalpas; no hundred thousand million ten-thousand kalpas.”

The Buddha said: “The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is a light without limit. The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: after countless kalpas, and again countless kalpas upon countless kalpas, and countless kalpas past all reckoning of kalpas — the kalpas are countless, and there is never a time of darkness. The land of Immeasurable Purity and all its heavens never have a time of decay. And why? Because the life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is exceedingly long and the land is most excellent; that is why it is so.”

The Buddha said: “The honored life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: after kalpas beyond number, kalpas that are ever countless, he has no time of parinirvana. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, teaching in the world, wishes to deliver all the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, and wishes to bring them all to be reborn in his land and all to attain the path of nirvana. All those who practice as bodhisattvas he wishes to make Buddhas, every one. And when they have become Buddhas, he causes them all in turn to teach again the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the eight directions, above and below, and again wishes them all to become Buddhas. And when they become Buddhas, they again teach countless devas and humans and crawling creatures, causing them all to attain the path of nirvana. All those whom he teaches as disciples, in turn teach one another and in turn deliver one another, until they attain the paths of the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha. Turning and delivering one another, they all attain the path of nirvana, all in this way.

The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity has never yet wished to pass into parinirvana. The deliverance wrought by the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, turning thus, abides again for countless kalpas — countless kalpas, past all reckoning of kalpas, and never a time of parinirvana. The countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the eight directions, above and below, who are born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity cannot be counted. Those who become arhats and attain the path of nirvana are also countless, past all reckoning.

The grace and virtue of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and all that he gives, extend through the eight directions, above and below, without end or limit, most deep and greatly immeasurable; the excellence and goodness of it cannot be spoken. The scriptures and the path brought forth by the wisdom and teaching of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity are proclaimed throughout the eight directions, above and below — countless, in the heavens and the world below, very many beyond numbering. The number of those scriptures is very great, past all reckoning, wholly without limit.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “Do you wish to know whether the life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is without limit?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “I wish indeed to hear and know it.”
